components: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence and Cognitive Science

y1-algorithms.name: Algorithms and Data Structures (AI)
y1-algorithms.entry: Advised: Students are expected to have knowledge and programming skills sufficient to complete the Imperative Programming for AI course (WBAI003-05).
y1-algorithms.content:
This course builds on the course Imperative Programming. We will cover fundamental data structures and algorithms from three areas: linear structures (stacks, queues, linked lists), trees and graphs. For each structure we will see its definition, an implementation and applications. Further attention will be paid to 'good programming', i.e. the design of correct, efficient and understandable programs and their documentation.

Besides lectures there will be tutorials with theoretical exercises and lab sessions where you will develop your own programs.

The main programming language that will be used in this course is C, which will be introduced in the first lecture. We use C because it is an easy language, and it makes both the data structures and the algorithms very explicit, when compared to higher level languages such as Python.

y1-autonomous.name: Autonomous Systems
y1-autonomous.content:
In this course, we explore essential topics for Autonomous Systems such as embodied cognition, robotics, sensing, locomotion, control architectures, and machine learning. The course will cover various fundamental concepts and examples relating to robotics, including kinematics, behaviour-based control, interactive learning, symbol grounding and social robotics.

Theoretical concepts will be introduced and explained during the lectures, and will be discussed in relation to real world examples during the tutorials. Practicals are provided to support students in practical exercises that cover concepts including Braitenberg vehicles, mechanics, hybrid control, and reinforcement learning.

y1-calculus.name: Calculus for Artificial Intelligence
y1-calculus.entry:
- The course unit assumes only prior knowledge acquired from Mathematics B (preferably) or Mathematics A as taught in pre-university programmes (VWO) at Dutch secondary schools (or equivalent).
- The course unit is followed by, and prepares students for, various AI BSc. courses (e.g. Linear Algebra & Multivariable Calculus and Signals & Systems) in which the learning objectives attained are required as prior knowledge.
- This course is an entry requirement for the following course: Signals and Systems [WBAI016-05]
y1-calculus.content:
In this course, basic concepts (and skills) in the area of calculus are discussed.

The course starts with refreshing and improving the basic mathematical skills (BMS) during period 1a. 'Extra' lectures are given to bridge the gap between Mathematics A and Mathematics B, since topics like e-power, natural logarithm, sin and cos may not be part of the Mathematics A curriculum at Dutch secondary schools. 

A diagnostic test is held:
Students who score less than 14 out of 20 points are required to follow additional BMS practice sessions. Later in period 1a, the second BMS test is taken. The highest score for the two BMS tests counts for the final grade (see below).

In the actual Calculus course, which mainly runs in period 1b(*), real functions of one real variable are treated: standard and composed functions, models, limits, derivatives, extreme values, Taylor expansions, and integrals (applications and techniques). Subsequently complex numbers are introduced, an imaginary extension of the real numbers. Finally, differential equations are solved to describe processes in physics, economy, medical sciences, etc.
This topic includes: initial value problems, directional fields, equilibrium solutions and stability, separation of variables, variation of constants, homogeneous and inhomogeneous equations, and conversion of complex solutions into real-valued solutions.

The material is illustrated through examples that focus on the applications of mathematical techniques.
(*) part of the actual Calculus course may be moved to period 1a.

y1-cognitive.name: Cognitive Psychology
y1-cognitive.content: This module is an introduction to the most important concepts and research results in cognitive psychology. Subjects to be dealt with include perception, focused and divided attention, working memory, long-term memory, knowledge, intelligence, reasoning, logical thinking, judgment and decision making, and consciousness.

y1-fundamentals.name: Fundamental Artificial Intelligence
y1-fundamentals.content:
This course offers a comprehensive introduction to the theory and practice of Artificial Intelligence, structured around six key areas of the field: machine learning, automated reasoning, multi-agent systems, problem solving, perception, and natural language processing. It provides students with foundational knowledge and practical skills to design intelligent systems capable of operating in diverse and complex environments.
• Problem Solving:
Students will learn core methods for decision-making and planning, including various search algorithms (uninformed, informed, local, and adversarial) and constraint satisfaction techniques. These methods enable agents to solve structured problems efficiently and adaptively.
• Automated Reasoning:
The course covers the basics of knowledge representation and inference, focusing on how agents can reason logically and draw conclusions from available data, even in uncertain or dynamic scenarios.
• Multi-Agent Systems:
Topics include agents interacting in shared environments, especially in adversarial settings. Students will explore strategic decision-making, coordination, and competition between autonomous entities.
• Machine Learning:
While the course does not provide in-depth coverage of learning algorithms, it introduces the concept of agents adapting their behavior based on experience, and lays the groundwork for future study in machine learning.
• Perception:
The course introduces the concept of agents operating under conditions of partial observability and uncertainty, requiring them to interpret incomplete or noisy information about their environment.
• Natural Language Processing (NLP):
Basic concepts are introduced to demonstrate how intelligent systems can process and respond to human language, motivating further exploration in this area.
By the end of the course, students will be able to design autonomous agents capable of decision-making and problem-solving in a variety of settings, from fully observable environments to complex, uncertain, and adversarial domains.

y1-linguistics.name: General Linguistics
y1-linguistics.entry:
No prior knowledge is assumed.

This course is an entry requirement for the course Structural Analysis of Language for Cognitive Modelling [WBAI052-05] & Human Language Learning [WBAI072-05].
y1-linguistics.content:
The use of language is a cognitive skill unique to humans, and language is a vital element of AI technology, including large language models and speech recognition systems. This module provides an introduction to the fundamental knowledge necessary to work effectively with language in AI, drawing from various subfields of linguistics including phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics and sociolinguistics. 

In the module, participants will explore the relationship between the commonly acknowledged perspective in contemporary linguistics that views language as a rule-based, symbolic system and the statistical approaches to language modelling that are common in AI. Participants will work with data from a range of languages to understand cross-linguistic similarities and differences. Throughout the course, emphasis will be placed on how linguistic knowledge can be applied in AI and in
modelling cognition.

y1-programming.name: Imperative Programming (for AI)
y1-programming.content:
This course covers the basics of programming for the Artificial Intelligence programme, including topics such as variables, conditionals, controls, functions, arrays, strings, and recursion.

Weekly assignments provide you with the opportunity to test your mastery of the topics covered up until that week. Final
assessment takes the form of a digital exam, where programming assignments have to be completed within a two hour time window.

y1-intro-ai.name: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence and Cognitive Science
y1-intro-ai.content:
This module provides an overview of the subjects dealt within the Artificial Intelligence program. Human and artificial intelligence will be approached from different angles, concentrating on the following topics: what is intelligence, differences and similarities between brains and computers, remembering and forgetting, language and natural
language processing, reasoning, different forms of learning, neural networks, machine learning, consciousness and the philosophical problem of body and mind. The focus in all these topics will be on the question of formalization: how can we gain a better understanding of a phenomenon by creating a formal description of it, whether in a mathematical, computational or logical formalism.

y1-logic.name: Introduction to Logic (AI)
y1-logic.content:
The course provides an introduction to formal logic, the discipline underpinning much of the symbolic approaches to AI. 
It covers: the languages, syntactic normal forms, semantics and proof theory (in natural deduction systems) of propositional and first-order logic.

y1-neuroscience.name: Introduction to Neuroscience
y1-neuroscience.content: This course introduces students to the biological foundations of behavior, perception, and cognition, with a focus on their relevance to artificial intelligence. Students will explore the structure and function of the nervous system, neural communication, sensory processing, and brain mechanisms. The course draws connections between neural principles and AI concepts such as neural networks, embodiment, and cognitive architectures, laying the groundwork for biologically inspired approaches to AI.

y1-linear.name: Linear Algebra and Multivariable Calculus
y1-linear.entry:
Recommended prior knowledge: the course unit assumes prior knowledge acquired from Calculus for Artificial Intelligence (WBAI048-05) or Calculus for Computing Science (WBCS036-05), in the 1st year of the BSc's of AI & CS.

This course is an entry requirement for the following course:
- Introduction to Machine Learning [WBAI056-05]
y1-linear.content:
In this course, first basic concepts and skills in the area of linear algebra are discussed.

Subsequently, functions of one variable are extended to multi-variable functions, with topics such as: partial derivatives, directional derivatives, gradients, extremes of a multi-variable function and multi-dimensional integration.

The material is illustrated through examples that focus on the applications of mathematical techniques.

y1-statistics.name: Statistics
y1-statistics.entry:
No prior knowledge is assumed.

This course is an entry requirement for Data Analytics and communication (WBAI011-05) and the Bachelor’s Project [WBAI901-15].
y1-statistics.content: This course covers the basics of statistics, focusing on how to draw conclusions about population characteristics from sample data. The R programming environment helps in the analysis of sample data, simulation of statistical concepts, and visualization of data.

y2-advanced-logic.name: Advanced Logic
y2-advanced-logic.content:
In this course, students learn that there are several other logics than the classical propositional and predicate logic that they know from the introductory logic course. Indeed, each context and application area requires a developer to think about which type of logic is appropriate to model the given situation, for example, in order to prove a program to be correct or to design communication protocols among software agents.

The topics of the course include: proof by induction on the natural numbers and on the construction of well-formed formulas; many-valued logics, including three-valued, four-valued, and fuzzy logic; several types of modal logic, including propositional and first-order modal logic, as well as temporal logics; the method of tableau proofs for propositional logic and several modal logics; soundness and completeness proofs; and nonmonotonic reasoning, especially default logic, including its procedural semantics.

y2-architectures.name: Architectures of Intelligence
y2-architectures.entry:
Recommended prior knowledge: Some programming experience and introduction in either cognitive psychology or cognitive science; typically Imperative Programming, Cognitive Psychology, and Introduction to the Brain or Introduction to Neuroscience.

This course is an entry requirement for the course Cognitive Modelling Practical [WBAI020-05].
y2-architectures.content:
An architecture of intelligence is an environment to simulate human intelligent behavior. Architectures are implementations of general theories of cognition that have the goal to cover the full spectrum of human cognition. The goals of this course are to give insight in these architectures and their scientific status, to gain some experience in
building models using an architecture, and to compare simulation results to empirical data.

y2-data.name: Data Analytics and Communication
y2-data.entry: [b]It's strongly recommended to have passed Statistics WBAI049-05 (or at least a final grade of 5.0) before taking this course.[/b]
y2-data.content: While people could easily be replaced in running statistical tests on that, interpreting the results and communicating those to others are much more difficult skills that cannot be mastered by a computer. In this course we develop these crucial skills. We think together about how to go about asking good questions for solving a scientific or societal problem, how to conduct reproducible research, and how to communicate the obtained results. This highly interactive course will provide the student with crucial skills for successfully completing a Bachelor project and for being an effective data scientist.

y2-ethics.name: Ethics in Artificial Intelligence
y2-ethics.entry: Advised: A grounded knowledge about topics in Artificial Intelligence, to provide for a healthy basis for discussion. Knowledge from Philosophy of AI and Cognition, Introduction to Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning courses are examples of these topics.
y2-ethics.content:
This course investigates the societal impact of AI by offering an introduction to different ethical issues raised or amplified by the development of AI technologies. The course focuses on a different theme each week, among which: biases and algorithmic fairness; privacy issues; impact of large language models; and the spread of misinformation.
For each theme, the course answers the following questions: What is the issue? Is it specifically an AI issue? What
can be done about it?

y2-intro-ml.name: Introduction to Machine Learning (for AI)
y2-intro-ml.entry:
Recommended prior knowledge:
- Calculus for Artificial Intelligence [WBAI048-05] 
- Mathematical concepts: Matrices and Vector spaces, Hyperplanes, Eigenvalues/Eigenvectors, Gradients, Probability, Probability Distributions and Random Variables.

This course is an entry requirement for the following courses: 
- Uncertainty in Machine Learning (WBAI54-05)
- Neural Networks (WBAI28-05)
- Applied Machine Learning (WBAI065-05)
- AI Engineering Practical (WBAI080-10)
y2-intro-ml.content:
Machine Learning is about algorithms that learn from data. This course will cover the basics of learning algorithms. Students will learn supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning algorithms and techniques, the concept of a feature and how it is extracted, how to properly evaluate them, perform cross-validation, and their implementation using python and data processing pipelines like scikit-learn, numpy, pandas, keras, tensorflow, and pytorch.

Non-exhaustive selection of methods:
• Supervised: Linear regression, Linear Discriminant Analysis, Support Vector Machines, Decision Trees and Random Forests, Logistic Regression, Neural Networks and Deep Learning.
• Unsupervised: Principal Component Analysis, t-SNE, Multi-Dimensional Scaling, K-Means Clustering, DBSCAN.

y2-agents.name: Knowledge and Agent Systems
y2-agents.content: This course provides an introduction to knowledge and agent systems and their place in artificial intelligence. Knowledge systems are systems that can reason using a representation of their knowledge, while agent systems contain individuals that can perform actions. Topics addressed include cooperation and competition, knowledge, norms, argumentation, communication and evidence. In addition, specialized topics addressed in current research are addressed. The class includes lectures and lab exercises.

y2-applied-ml.name: Applied Machine Learning
y2-applied-ml.content:
This course covers the practicalities of using supervised and unsupervised Machine Learning methods to solve a problem. The practical is set up as an end-to-end project starting from project ideation, through data exploration, preprocessing and sanitization, to feature selection, model selection, hyperparameter optimization, model evaluation and finally model deployment to a demo environment. While the course does have lectures, most time is spent on practical work.

Students propose their own projects that align with their own passions, interests and knowledge, and will be advised on the feasibility and appropriateness for the course.

The course assumes familiarity with concepts from Introduction to Machine Learning, so those topics will not be revisited in detail. Instead, the emphasis will be on data preprocessing, working with and understanding some tools needed for Machine Learning projects (such as Pandas, NumPy and scikit-learn), and finally working with a tool to allow simple model deployment.

The course does not address the related topics of: model deployment in production, Machine Learning with big data, professionalized MLOps, or model monitoring.

y2-nlp.name: Natural Language Processing
y2-nlp.entry:
Assumed prior knowledge
- Introduction to Machine Learning (WBAI056)
y2-nlp.content: Recent improvements in natural language processing (NLP) have resulted in systems that can translate text, answer questions, and even hold spoken conversations with humans. The ability to effectively harness, employ, and analyze linguistic and textual data is a highly desirable skill for academic work, government, and the private sector. As people communicate almost everything in language, NLP applications are everywhere: web searches, advertising, emails, customer service, language translation, virtual agents, medical reports, and so on. This course will introduce students to the basics of NLP, covering standard frameworks for dealing with natural language as well as algorithms and techniques to solve various NLP problems, including recent deep learning approaches. Topics covered include language modeling, representation learning, text classification, Sequence-to-sequence modeling, machine translation, question answering, and others.

y2-oop.name: Object-Oriented Programming (for AI)
y2-oop.entry: [b]Strongly recommended prior knowledge:[/b] Students are assumed to have programming skills equivalent to passing the course Imperative Programming (for AI) [WBAI003-05].
y2-oop.content: This course continues on the path of Imperative Programming and Algorithms and Data Structures, and gives an introduction to object-oriented programming. In particular, principles of object oriented programming in Python will be discussed, including inheritance, polymorphism, and decorators, as well as more advanced notions such as common design patterns for object-oriented programming.

y2-philosophy.name: Philosophy of AI and Cognition
y2-philosophy.entry: Completion of the BA / Minor course Philosophy of Science and Logic or another introductory course on philosophy of science or cognitive science.
y2-philosophy.content:
The fields of artificial intelligence (AI) and cognitive science have been closely connected from the start. Cognitive science emerged in the 1950s as a project to provide a scientific, computational account of the human mind, whereas one of the aims of artificial intelligence has been to build systems that think like humans (or better). Therefore, notions such as ‘intelligence’, ‘cognition’ or ‘thinking’ are central to both fields. Both fields continue to thrive, but in recent years, we have especially witnessed an explosive growth of AI technology: AI is used for medical diagnosis, for composing music, for self-driving cars, and is becoming increasingly important for society. 

The study of AI and cognition involves many deeply philosophical questions: Can machines think and become conscious? What are the limits of AI? What is cognition or thinking? What can AI tell us about human cognition?  In this course, we study these and other questions by discussing both traditional literature on philosophy of AI and cognition, as well as more recent theoretical and philosophical developments.

y2-skills.name: Scientific Skills
y2-skills.entry: Recommended prior knowledge: Basic programming skills in Python, statistical knowledge and an overview of topics in cognitive psychology are recommended for this course.
y2-skills.content:
Students will acquire a number of scientific skills: They will learn how to find and evaluate relevant scientific literature, how to formulate a good scientific research question and test it through a well designed behavioral experiment, how to analyze and interpret the results, and how to communicate their research in written and oral form.

To this end the course consists of lectures and tutorials and the course is structured in 4 parts: plan, collect, analyze and present. The lectures will be workshops and theoretical introductions to the different part of the scientific method.

In the tutorials, students apply the knowledge gained from the lectures by working in small groups on their own research projects. Homework assignments help to progress through the research project and each project is concluded with a scientific presentation and a scientific article.

y2-signals.name: Signals and Systems (for AI)
y2-signals.entry:
Recommended prior knowledge:
- Linear Algebra and Multivariable Calculus [WBAI050-05]
- Programming knowledge comparable to Imperative Programming (WBAI003-05).
y2-signals.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) agents learn about their environment through signals. These signals can include images, sounds, text, and other types like medical, weather, communication, and financial data. To process them, systems perform tasks such as noise reduction, compression, and feature detection, helping AI agents understand the information better.

This course covers the fundamental concepts of signals and systems, focusing on their use in AI. Through weekly lectures, tutorials, and practicals, students will build a strong foundation in signal processing. The course covers the following topics:
- Time-Frequency Analysis
- Linear Time-Variant Systems and Filter Design
- Fourier, Laplace, and Z transforms.

y3-brain-modelling.name: Computational Modelling of the Brain
y3-brain-modelling.entry:
Recommended prior knowledge:
- Introduction to the Brain [WBAI026-05]
- Introduction to Machine Learning (for AI) [WBAI056-05]
y3-brain-modelling.content: Both humans and technology can be described as intelligent, but the connection between them is not always clear. In this course we will discuss aspects of intelligence as functional mechanisms in the brain, and use AI tools and techniques to implement and explore different components of the mind. We will combine theoretical concepts of intelligence like learning and memory with technical tools like reinforcement learning and neural networks to build computational models that reflect different aspects of how the brain thinks.

y3-neural.name: Neural Computation
y3-neural.entry:
Recommended prior knowledge:
This course assumes you are comfortable writing programs in your favourite programming language.
y3-neural.content:
This class will cover concepts and methods for building basic neural processing systems, scaling from neural encodings of sensory stimuli up to architectures that perform inference in self-organized networks of relations. In the homeworks you will build small systems following representational and architectural principles seen in the cerebral cortex. Emphasis will be placed on understanding principles and abstractions that are applicable to a variety of systems.

This course does not use or discuss backpropagation or deep networks or machine learning. Instead, it covers approaches seen in the brain, such as (1) explicit representations via population codes, (2) learning rules that depend only on locally available information, (2) relationships between variables encoded via areas whose neurons respond to combinations of variables, (3) pervasive bidirectional communication between areas, and (4) how the resulting computations can be robustly performed even with unreliable units.

y3-project.name: Bachelor's Project
y3-project.entry:
Mandatory entry requirements: 
- Start your Graduation process and have applied for your diploma in ProgressWWW. See the 
[url=https://student.portal.rug.nl/infonet/studenten/fse/programmes/bsc-ai/year-3/bachelor-s-project]Student Portal[/url] for more information. 
- Completion of the First year of the degree programme
- Data Analytics and Communication [WBAI011-05] (formerly named Data Science [WBAI064-05])
- Statistics (WBAI049-05)
- Completion of at least 135 ECTS from the AI bachelor programme (i.e., a study delay of max. 15 ECTS)
Practical implementation (Semester 2): early January a check will be done. At that time  you must have obtained at least 120 ECTS. 

Advised: Students are advised to take this course at the end of their bachelor's programme, as it's the finalising element. If they happen to have the requirements for the upcoming iteration, but do not expect to finish before the end of an iteration in a later semester, they should take the bachelor's project of that semester (so at the latest possible moment in their programme).
y3-project.content:
The Bachelor's project is the final activity of the Bachelor's programme. It includes tutorials on research skills and developing project management skills.
With regard to content, the project links up with one or more of the modules in the AI study programme. This means that in general, it will not be necessary to study much additional literature for the project and the emphasis will be more on the practical work.
Bachelor's Projects are performed within the AI department and are usually part of the research activities of the AI staff.

There are formal Graduation Regulations regarding the Bachelor's project. One of these regulations is that the project has to be finished within one semester.

At the start of the semester, students will choose from a pre-compiled list of Bachelor projects that are on offer that semester. Information on this will be presented in the first tutorial.

progression: The first year has 60 EC and no prescribed formal exam order. The dated catalogue distributes the courses across two semesters. Completed first-year Logic, Linear Algebra and Multivariable Calculus, and Calculus for AI respectively satisfy Advanced Logic, Introduction to Machine Learning and Signals and Systems.

The second year has 60 EC. Introduction to Machine Learning in the first semester precedes Applied Machine Learning in the second and supplies assumed background for Natural Language Processing. The earlier neuroscience course replaces Introduction to the Brain for the incoming cohort.

The programme page places the project in the second semester, with the 45 EC of other study distributed across the year. The two already catalogued Computational Neuroscience courses are in the first semester of 2026–2027. If that pattern continues, the student can take those 10 EC and 20 EC of approved minor study in the first semester, leaving 10 EC of minor study and Cognitive Neuroscience alongside the project. The exact split depends on future scheduling and approval. Completing the first two years gives 120 EC before year three, and completing 30 EC more before the project clears the 135 EC requirement. The bachelor project also requires all year-one courses, Data Analytics and Communication, Statistics and study-plan submission. Complete project registration steps. The three specialisation courses count 15 EC in total. The adopted curriculum introduces Cognitive Neuroscience from 2027–2028, before the incoming student reaches year three in 2028–2029. The 2026–2027 two-course transitional variant is for earlier cohorts. The detailed future timetable is subject to catalogue confirmation.
